relations.myth: Ọya’s nine children and masked last-born
relations.note: Ọya bears Egúngún as her ninth child, whose face or voice is abnormal.
relations.source: Babayemi, Egúngún among the Ọ̀yọ́ Yoruba

relations.myth: Ọya conducts and controls the dead
relations.note: Ọya rules, drives, and sends back the ancestral eguns through dance and ritual authority.
Drewal interprets Egúngún’s wind-producing whirls as related to Ọya’s whirlwind.
Egúngún manifestations appear during or in relation to Ọya festivals in Ọ̀yọ́.
relations.source: Babayemi, Egúngún among the Ọ̀yọ́ Yoruba

relations.note: In a Brazilian variant, Ṣàngó fathers nine children; the ninth is Egungum.
Ṣàngó founds, commands, domesticates, or incorporates Egúngún into Ọ̀yọ́ royal religion.
Eguns pursue Ṣàngó until Ọya intervenes and rescues him.
Egúngún manifestations appear during or in relation to Ṣàngó festivals in Ọ̀yọ́.
relations.source: Babayemi, Egúngún among the Ọ̀yọ́ Yoruba

relations.myth: Omolu grants Ọya authority over eguns
relations.note: Omolu grants Ọya authority over the dead, placing eguns under her ritual control.
Ifá restores dead children whose terrible faces are veiled; they become Egúngún.
Divination prescribes Ọya’s fertility offerings, explains masquerade customs, and orders ancestral invocation.
Exu mediates movement and offerings within the broader ritual order surrounding Egúngún ancestors.
Egúngún and Orò are paired but distinct; Egúngún appears publicly while Orò is nocturnal and restrictive.

relations.myth: Divine ordering of ayé and ọ̀run
relations.note: Modern narratives place the ancestral institution within Olódùmarè’s ordering of the visible and divine realms.
